passage:
After a video of him slipping in the changing room went round Year 10, Felix stopped eating in the canteen. At home in Bradford, his dad had been out of work since spring.
The only place anyone asked how he was doing was a voice channel on a game server. Older players, patient, funny. "You're one of us, brother." "They laugh at lads like you because they want you small." Nobody explained who "they" were. It didn't matter. For the first time in months, Felix felt part of something.
On Thursday one of them said, "Don't tell your mum about us. She won't get it."
Felix told Liam at the bus stop, half laughing. Liam didn't laugh. "Mate, that's the bit that's wrong."
That evening Felix left the server and told his mum everything. She switched off the kettle and sat down beside him. "Thank you for telling me. You're not in trouble. We'll go into school together tomorrow."

qa.q: Where did anyone ask Felix how he was doing?
qa.a: Only in a voice channel on a game server.

qa.q: What was Felix feeling that made the voice channel so appealing?
qa.a: Felix felt humiliated after the video and unseen at home, so being called "brother" and part of something filled a real hunger to belong.

qa.q: Which moment was the turning point, and what did Felix do right?
qa.a: Being told to hide the group from his mum was the warning sign; Felix left the server and told his mum everything that same evening.

qa.q: How did Felix's mum respond when he told her?
qa.a: She switched off the kettle, sat beside him, thanked him, told him he was not in trouble and planned to go into school with him the next day.

grounding: A humiliated teenage boy is drawn to online voices offering brotherhood and an enemy, and when asked for secrecy he leaves and tells his mum, who responds at once.

passage:
The counsellor's room at Neelam's school smelled of marker pens. Preeti ma'am had seen the slogans in her notebook: "Rise." "They took everything." "Sisters stand together."
"Where did these come from?" she asked, not angrily.
Neelam shrugged, then couldn't stop. How Mr Verma had read her failed maths marks aloud to the whole class in July and everyone laughed. How afterwards she'd found a channel, then a Saturday meeting behind the bus depot. Older girls who called her sister. Who said her anger meant she was awake. Who told her exactly whose fault her life was.
"It's the first time anyone said I matter," Neelam said. Her voice cracked.
Preeti ma'am didn't argue about the slogans. "Being laughed at like that hurts. You deserved better." She pulled a chair closer. "Let's talk about the maths, and about what you'd want to build. And I'll call your mother today so she can help too."

qa.q: What did Mr Verma read aloud to the class?
qa.a: Mr Verma read Neelam's failed maths marks aloud to the whole class.

qa.q: What does Neelam's cracked voice show about what drew her in?
qa.a: It shows the pull was the feeling of mattering after being humiliated, much more than any idea the group preached.

qa.q: What did Preeti ma'am do that kept Neelam talking?
qa.a: Preeti ma'am listened without arguing, named the hurt of being laughed at, and moved to practical help, including calling Neelam's mother that day.

qa.q: What would change if Preeti ma'am had scolded Neelam about the slogans?
qa.a: Neelam would likely have shut down and felt that only the group understood her, making the pull stronger.

grounding: A humiliated teenage girl is pulled to a group offering sisterhood, purpose and someone to blame, and a counsellor responds to the hurt beneath it.
